texts.title: Keeping the lights on the coast

paragraphs.text: For most of recorded history, a ship approaching land at night had little to guide it except the stars, the depth of the water beneath the keel and whatever fires happened to be burning on shore. The earliest purpose-built lights were exactly that: open fires of wood or coal kept alight on a tower or a headland, often by people who were paid irregularly and who had every reason to let the flames die down on a wet night. Such fires consumed enormous quantities of fuel, produced more smoke than light, and could not be distinguished from the ordinary glow of a harbour town, so a captain who saw one could never be entirely sure what he was looking at.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Enclosing the flame was the first real advance. Once lanterns with glass panes were fixed at the top of towers in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the light was protected from wind and rain, and candles, then oil lamps, replaced the open fire. The difficulty was that a lamp radiates in every direction, including upwards into the sky and downwards into the tower, and only a small fraction of what it produces travels towards the sea. Early attempts to solve this placed polished metal reflectors behind each lamp, which helped a great deal but tarnished quickly in the salty air and had to be cleaned by hand several times a night.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The decisive change came from optics rather than from better fuel. In the 1820s a French engineer proposed a lens built not as a single thick piece of glass, which would have been impossibly heavy, but as a series of concentric rings, each shaped to bend the light by exactly the right amount. The rings gathered the light that would otherwise have escaped and concentrated it into a horizontal beam, so that a single lamp could be seen at a distance that would previously have required dozens. Within a few decades the design had been adopted by almost every maritime nation, and the largest versions, taller than a person, were being made in only a handful of workshops.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: A concentrated beam created a new problem that turned out to be an opportunity. If every light shone steadily, a navigator could not tell one tower from the next, and mistaking one headland for another was a common cause of shipwreck. Engineers therefore mounted the lens on a rotating base, which turned the steady glow into a sequence of flashes, and each station was assigned its own rhythm: two flashes every ten seconds for one, a long flash followed by darkness for another. The pattern became the light’s signature, printed in the lists carried on every ship, and a captain who counted the seconds between flashes knew where he was without seeing the coast at all.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Keeping such a system working required people, and the keeper’s life has attracted more attention than the technology. Keepers wound the clockwork that rotated the lens, trimmed wicks, cleaned glass and kept a written log of the weather and passing ships. On remote rock stations a crew of three would spend weeks at a time without leaving, relieved by boat when the sea allowed, and the rule that there should always be three people rather than two is said to have been introduced after an isolated station was found with one keeper dead and the other unable to cope. Whether that story is accurate matters less than the fact that it was widely believed.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Electricity and then automation removed the keepers over the course of the twentieth century. Electric lamps were brighter and needed less attention, and once lights could be monitored from a distance and switched on by sensors that detected nightfall, the case for staffing them weakened. The last crews were withdrawn in many countries during the 1980s and 1990s, and towers that had once housed families became unoccupied machinery, visited by maintenance teams a few times a year. Some were sold as holiday homes; others, on exposed rocks, were simply left to the weather.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Satellite navigation has raised the question of whether the lights are needed at all. A modern vessel knows its position to within a few metres, displays it on a screen and can follow a route without anyone looking out of the window. Several authorities have reduced the range of their lights or switched off those that no longer mark a genuine hazard, and the savings are real. Yet maritime agencies have been reluctant to go further, because satellite signals can fail, be jammed or be imitated, and a light that depends on nothing but electricity and a lens remains the one aid that a captain can check with his own eyes.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The lighthouse has therefore become a backup rather than a primary guide, which is an unusual position for a technology to occupy. Most systems that are overtaken disappear; this one has been retained precisely because it is old, simple and independent of the systems that replaced it. Its survival says something about how safety is designed at sea, where the most valued equipment is often not the most advanced but the one least likely to fail at the same moment as everything else. The towers that remain are, in that sense, less a monument to the past than an insurance policy for the present.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: Among animals that have been studied for signs of intelligence, the octopus is the one that least resembles us. Its last common ancestor with the vertebrates lived more than five hundred million years ago and was probably a small, worm-like creature with a very simple nervous system, which means that whatever the octopus has achieved in the way of problem-solving, it has achieved along an entirely separate evolutionary route. For researchers interested in whether intelligence is a single thing that evolution keeps rediscovering or a collection of different solutions to different problems, that independence is what makes the animal so valuable to study.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The anatomy alone is enough to unsettle assumptions. An octopus has around five hundred million neurons, a number comparable to that of a dog, but roughly two-thirds of them are located not in the head but in the arms. Each arm can taste what it touches through receptors in its suckers, can respond to a stimulus without instructions from the brain, and will continue to reach and grasp for a time even after it has been separated from the body. The central brain appears to issue broad commands, leaving the arms to work out the details of how those commands are carried out.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Laboratory reports of octopus behaviour were for a long time treated as anecdotes. Animals were said to have escaped from their tanks at night, crossed the floor to a neighbouring tank, eaten the occupants and returned before morning; others squirted water deliberately at particular keepers, or switched off lights by aiming a jet at the bulb. Such stories are hard to verify and easy to exaggerate, and serious researchers were cautious about repeating them. One much-repeated account, in which an animal was said to have darkened a laboratory by aiming at the same lamp night after night, has never been traced to a reliable source. What changed was the arrival of controlled experiments in which the same task was given to many individuals and the results recorded systematically.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Those experiments confirmed much of what the anecdotes suggested. Octopuses learn to open screw-top jars to reach food inside, and they learn faster after watching another octopus do it, although they are not social animals and have little obvious reason to learn from each other. They can distinguish between individual humans, approaching some and avoiding others, even when the people are dressed identically. In maze studies they remember routes for days, and some individuals appear to explore objects that offer no reward at all, a behaviour that in other animals is usually interpreted as a form of play.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The short life of the octopus is the puzzle at the centre of the field. Most species live for only one or two years, the mother dies soon after her eggs hatch, and the young receive no instruction of any kind. In mammals and birds, large brains are generally associated with long lives and long periods of dependence on parents, during which learning is thought to pay for the enormous cost of maintaining neural tissue. The octopus has the brain without the childhood, and no fully satisfying explanation has yet been offered for why natural selection favoured such an expensive organ in an animal that has so little time to use it. Some researchers suspect that the question itself assumes too much about why brains evolve in the first place.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: One proposal links the answer to the loss of the shell. The ancestors of the octopus were protected by hard outer casings, as some of their relatives still are, and giving up that protection made the animal fast and flexible but extremely vulnerable. A soft body that can be eaten by almost anything must constantly assess its surroundings, find or build shelter and change its colour and texture to match the background. On this account, intelligence did not arise to exploit a long life but to survive a dangerous one, and the brain is the price of having no armour.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Studying such an animal raises questions that researchers working on mammals rarely face. Standard tests of learning were designed for creatures that see, move and are motivated in ways similar to rats or monkeys, and an octopus may fail them for reasons that have nothing to do with ability: it may not care about the reward, or may prefer to explore the apparatus rather than use it. Designing fair experiments requires first understanding what matters to the animal, which is itself a research problem, and several apparently negative results from earlier decades are now regarded as tests of the wrong question. Some laboratories now spend weeks watching an animal before testing it at all, simply to learn what it pays attention to.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The ethical position has shifted accordingly. Several countries now include octopuses in legislation that protects animals used in research, requiring that experiments be justified and that suffering be minimised, protections that were formerly reserved for vertebrates. The change followed reviews of the evidence that these animals can experience pain rather than merely react to damage. It has also affected discussions about farming octopuses for food, which would involve keeping solitary, curious animals in crowded tanks, and which a number of scientists have argued against on the grounds that no system of confinement could meet their needs.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: Can a city have too many visitors?

paragraphs.text: A generation ago, the problem facing most historic cities was a shortage of visitors rather than a surplus. Tourism was welcomed as a source of income for places whose traditional industries had declined, and local authorities competed to attract airlines, cruise ships and conference organisers. That consensus has broken down in a remarkably short time. In a number of popular destinations, residents now complain that their neighbourhoods have been turned into stage sets, and some authorities have begun to restrict the very flows they once spent heavily to encourage. The debate that has followed is often conducted in slogans, which is a pity, because the evidence is more interesting than either side’s rhetoric.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Ingrid Solberg, an economist, argues that the difficulty lies less in the total number of visitors than in how unevenly they are spread. In most of the cities she has examined, the great majority of tourists visit a small central district for a few hours, often on the same days and at the same times, while other neighbourhoods see almost none. Annual figures, she points out, can therefore look moderate while particular streets are overwhelmed for part of every day. Policies that aim to cut the overall total, in her view, will do less good than those that shift visits to other areas and other seasons, though she concedes that visitors’ preferences are stubborn.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The housing market is where Tomás Ferreira, a geographer, locates the most serious harm. When flats in a central district can earn more as short-term rentals for visitors than as homes for residents, owners have a strong incentive to convert them, and in some neighbourhoods a large share of the housing stock has changed use within a decade. Rents rise, long-standing residents move out, and the shops that served them are replaced by businesses aimed at people who will stay for three nights. Ferreira describes the outcome as a district that remains full of people but has lost its population, and he regards limits on short-term letting as more urgent than any restriction on arrivals.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that tourists are the principal cause. Priya Raman, who studies urban policy, notes that the neighbourhoods now described as damaged by tourism were often already changing through ordinary processes of rising property prices and the departure of families to the suburbs. Visitors, she suggests, are a visible and convenient target, since they do not vote in local elections and cannot complain about how they are described. That does not mean the pressures are imaginary, but it does mean that a policy aimed only at visitors may leave the underlying causes untouched, and she is sceptical that a cap on arrivals would bring back the residents who have left.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: A further complication is that the income from tourism is distributed very unevenly. Hotels, airlines and tour operators based elsewhere may capture a large part of what visitors spend, while the costs of cleaning streets, managing crowds and maintaining monuments fall on the local budget. Several cities have introduced charges on overnight stays or entry fees for particular districts, partly to raise money and partly to discourage the shortest visits, which bring the least income and much of the congestion. How far such charges alter behaviour is disputed; they certainly raise revenue, and the revenue is at least visible to residents in a way that the benefits of tourism often are not.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Daniel Okafor, who has studied cruise traffic, draws attention to the form of travel that produces the sharpest peaks. A large ship can land several thousand passengers in a port for a single day, and because most of their meals and accommodation are provided on board, the city receives the crowds with relatively little of the spending. He argues that ports should negotiate the number and timing of ship calls as they would any other use of public infrastructure, and he points to harbours that have spread arrivals across the week without any loss of income. What he does not support is an outright ban, which in his view would simply move the ships to a neighbouring port with fewer controls.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: What these positions have in common is a shift from asking how many visitors a city can hold to asking which visitors, where and when. A limit on numbers is simple to announce and easy to understand, but it treats a cyclist who spends a week in a family guesthouse and a day visitor who spends an afternoon in the busiest square as the same kind of pressure, which they plainly are not. Instruments that distinguish between them, whether through pricing, planning rules or the timing of transport, are harder to design and to explain, and they are also more likely to achieve what residents actually want.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The honest answer to the question in the title is therefore yes, but not in the sense usually intended. A city can have too many visitors in one street at one hour and too few in the next district, and too many flats let to strangers while it lacks homes for its own teachers and nurses. Treating tourism as a single quantity to be increased or reduced has served neither the visitors nor the residents well. The cities that have made most progress are those that stopped counting arrivals and started measuring what the arrivals were doing to the places they came to see.
paragraphs.label: H

topic.en: Three texts: how lighthouses survived automation and satellites, what makes octopus intelligence unusual, and the argument about whether a city can have too many visitors.
topic.kk: Үш мәтін: маяктар автоматтандыру мен спутниктен қалай аман қалды, сегізаяқтың ақылы несімен ерекше және қалада туристер тым көп бола ма деген талқы.
topic.ru: Три текста: как маяки пережили автоматизацию и спутники, чем необычен интеллект осьминога и спор о том, может ли в городе быть слишком много туристов.

items.quote: If every light shone steadily, a navigator could not tell one tower from the next
items.prompt: an explanation of why a light that never changes could put ships at risk

explanation.en: A steady light made one tower impossible to tell from the next, and confusing headlands caused wrecks — paragraph D → D.
explanation.kk: Бірқалыпты жарық бір мұнараны екіншісінен ажыратуға мүмкіндік бермеген, ал мүйістерді шатастыру апатқа әкелген — D абзацы → D.
explanation.ru: Ровный свет не давал отличить одну башню от другой, а путаница мысов вела к крушениям — абзац D → D.

items.quote: not as a single thick piece of glass, which would have been impossibly heavy, but as a series of concentric rings
items.prompt: a reference to a design that avoided an excessive weight

explanation.en: A lens of rings instead of one thick piece of glass that would have been “impossibly heavy” — paragraph C. B also mentions glass, but only the lantern panes → C.
explanation.kk: Бір қалың шыны орнына сақиналардан жасалған линза, ал қалың шыны «impossibly heavy» болар еді — C абзацы. B абзацында да шыны бар, бірақ ол фонарь әйнегі → C.
explanation.ru: Линза из колец вместо одного толстого стекла, которое было бы «impossibly heavy», — абзац C. Абзац B тоже про стекло, но про остекление фонаря → C.

items.quote: could not be distinguished from the ordinary glow of a harbour town
items.prompt: the reason early lights were hard to identify from the sea

explanation.en: A fire on a tower “could not be distinguished from the ordinary glow of a harbour town” — paragraph A → A.
explanation.kk: Мұнарадағы от «ordinary glow of a harbour town» дегеннен ерекшеленбеген — A абзацы → A.
explanation.ru: Костёр на башне не отличался от «ordinary glow of a harbour town» — абзац A → A.

items.quote: Some were sold as holiday homes
items.prompt: a mention of what happened to some buildings once no one needed to live in them

explanation.en: Once the keepers left, some towers “were sold as holiday homes” — paragraph F. H is about the role of the towers, not the buildings → F.
explanation.kk: Күзетшілер кеткен соң кейбір мұнаралар «holiday homes» ретінде сатылған — F абзацы. H абзацы мұнаралардың рөлі туралы, ғимарат туралы емес → F.
explanation.ru: После ухода смотрителей часть башен продали как «holiday homes» — абзац F. Абзац H тоже о судьбе башен, но о роли, а не о зданиях → F.

groups.instruction: Text 1 has eight paragraphs, A–H. Which paragraph contains the following information? Write the correct letter, A–H.

items.quote: Such fires consumed enormous quantities of fuel, produced more smoke than light
items.prompt: Keeping an open fire burning on a tower was an economical way of producing light.

explanation.en: The fires “consumed enormous quantities of fuel” and gave more smoke than light — the opposite of economical → FALSE.
explanation.kk: Оттар «consumed enormous quantities of fuel», жарықтан гөрі түтін көп берген — «үнемді» дегенге қарама-қайшы → FALSE.
explanation.ru: Костры «consumed enormous quantities of fuel» и давали больше дыма, чем света — это противоположно «экономично» → FALSE.

items.quote: tarnished quickly in the salty air and had to be cleaned by hand several times a night
items.prompt: The salty atmosphere meant that the reflectors had to be polished repeatedly during the night.

explanation.en: “tarnished quickly in the salty air and had to be cleaned by hand several times a night” — the same idea reworded → TRUE.
explanation.kk: «tarnished quickly in the salty air and had to be cleaned by hand several times a night» — сол мағына басқа сөзбен → TRUE.
explanation.ru: «tarnished quickly in the salty air and had to be cleaned by hand several times a night» — то же самое другими словами → TRUE.

items.quote: the largest versions, taller than a person, were being made in only a handful of workshops
items.prompt: The French engineer who proposed the new lens also manufactured the first examples himself.

explanation.en: We only learn that the lenses were made in a few workshops, not who made the first ones. It is not FALSE — nothing contradicts it → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Линзаларды бірнеше шеберханада жасағаны ғана айтылған; алғашқыларын кім жасағаны жоқ. Бұл FALSE емес: мәтін бұған қарсы айтпайды → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: Сказано лишь, что линзы делали в нескольких мастерских; кто изготовил первые — не сказано. Это не FALSE: текст не спорит с утверждением → NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: The pattern became the light’s signature
items.prompt: Sailors could identify a particular station from the rhythm of its flashes.

explanation.en: The pattern “became the light’s signature”, and counting the seconds told a captain where he was → TRUE.
explanation.kk: Жарқыл ырғағы маяктың «signature» болған, капитан жарқылдар арасындағы секундтан қайда екенін білген → TRUE.
explanation.ru: Ритм вспышек стал «signature» маяка, а капитан по секундам между вспышками узнавал, где он → TRUE.

items.quote: is said to have been introduced after an isolated station was found with one keeper dead and the other unable to cope
items.prompt: The rule requiring three keepers on a station followed an official inquiry.
keywords: is said to have been introduced

explanation.en: The text reports a story (“is said”), but nothing about an official inquiry either way. Do not confuse with FALSE → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Мәтін әңгімені жеткізеді («is said»), бірақ ресми тексеру туралы ештеңе жоқ. FALSE-пен шатастырмаңыз → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: Текст передаёт рассказ («is said»), но о расследовании ничего нет — ни «да», ни «нет». Не путайте с FALSE → NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: because satellite signals can fail, be jammed or be imitated
items.prompt: Satellite signals are interfered with deliberately more often than they fail for technical reasons.

explanation.en: The text lists the risks — failure, jamming, imitation — but never says which happens more often → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Мәтін қауіптерді тізеді — ақау, кедергі, жалған сигнал, — бірақ қайсысы жиі болатынын салыстырмайды → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: Текст перечисляет риски — сбой, глушение, подмена, — но не сравнивает, что случается чаще. Сравнения нет → NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: candles, then oil lamps, replaced the open fire
items.prompt: Inside the first glazed lanterns, candles and later 11 ____ took over from burning wood or coal.

items.quote: a captain who counted the seconds between flashes knew where he was
items.prompt: A navigator could fix his position by timing the intervals between 12 ____.

explanation.en: “counted the seconds between flashes” → flashes; “timing the intervals” paraphrases “counted the seconds”.
explanation.kk: «counted the seconds between flashes» → flashes: «timing the intervals» — «counted the seconds» дегеннің басқаша айтылуы.
explanation.ru: «counted the seconds between flashes» → flashes: «timing the intervals» — перефраз «counted the seconds».

items.quote: switched on by sensors that detected nightfall
items.prompt: Unstaffed lights come on automatically because devices can sense 13 ____.

explanation.en: “switched on by sensors that detected nightfall” → nightfall; “sense” paraphrases “detected”.
explanation.kk: «switched on by sensors that detected nightfall» → nightfall; «sense» — «detected» сөзінің синонимі.
explanation.ru: «switched on by sensors that detected nightfall» → nightfall; «sense» — перефраз «detected».

groups.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS OR A NUMBER from Text 1 for each answer.

items.quote: was probably a small, worm-like creature with a very simple nervous system
items.prompt: The ancestor that octopuses share with vertebrates probably had a sophisticated nervous system.

explanation.en: The ancestor was “a small, worm-like creature with a very simple nervous system” — “very simple” contradicts “sophisticated” → FALSE.
explanation.kk: Ортақ ата — «a small, worm-like creature with a very simple nervous system»: «very simple» «sophisticated» дегенге қайшы → FALSE.
explanation.ru: Общий предок — «a small, worm-like creature with a very simple nervous system»: «very simple» противоречит «sophisticated» → FALSE.

items.quote: they learn faster after watching another octopus do it
items.prompt: In controlled studies, octopuses solved the jar task faster than other invertebrates did.

explanation.en: “learn faster” compares an octopus with itself before watching another, not with other invertebrates. That comparison is absent → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: «learn faster» — басқа сегізаяқты көргенге дейінгі өзімен салыстыру, басқа омыртқасыздармен емес. Мұндай салыстыру жоқ → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: «learn faster» — сравнение с самим собой до наблюдения за другим осьминогом, а не с другими беспозвоночными. Сравнения нет → NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: even when the people are dressed identically
items.prompt: Octopuses can recognise particular people even when those people are wearing the same clothes.

explanation.en: “They can distinguish between individual humans … even when the people are dressed identically” → TRUE.
explanation.kk: «They can distinguish between individual humans … even when the people are dressed identically» → TRUE.
explanation.ru: «They can distinguish between individual humans … even when the people are dressed identically» → TRUE.

items.quote: which a number of scientists have argued against on the grounds that no system of confinement could meet their needs
items.prompt: Farming octopuses for food has already been prohibited in several countries.

explanation.en: “Several countries” protect octopuses in research, and scientists argue against farming — but no ban on farming is mentioned → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: «Several countries» сегізаяқты зерттеуде қорғайды; фермаға ғалымдар қарсы, бірақ фермаға тыйым туралы айтылмаған → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: «Several countries» защищают осьминогов в исследованиях; против фермы выступают учёные, но о запрете ферм не сказано → NOT GIVEN.

items.prompt: make use of a long 22 ____

explanation.en: “did not arise to exploit a long life but to survive a dangerous one” → life; “make use of” paraphrases “exploit”.
explanation.kk: «did not arise to exploit a long life but to survive a dangerous one» → life; «make use of» — «exploit» дегеннің синонимі.
explanation.ru: «did not arise to exploit a long life but to survive a dangerous one» → life; «make use of» — перефраз «exploit».

groups.instruction: Complete the summary below. Choose ONE WORD ONLY from Text 2 for each answer.

items.quote: serious researchers were cautious about repeating them
items.prompt: Stories of octopuses escaping from their tanks

explanation.en: Serious researchers were “cautious about repeating them” → A.
explanation.kk: Қашу туралы әңгімелерді ғалымдар айтуға сақтанған — «cautious about repeating them» → A.
explanation.ru: Истории о побегах серьёзные учёные пересказывать опасались — «cautious about repeating them» → A.

items.quote: they learn faster after watching another octopus do it
items.prompt: An octopus that has watched another one open a jar

explanation.en: “they learn faster after watching another octopus do it” → B.
explanation.kk: «they learn faster after watching another octopus do it» → B.
explanation.ru: «they learn faster after watching another octopus do it» → B.

items.quote: a behaviour that in other animals is usually interpreted as a form of play
items.prompt: Investigating objects that bring no benefit

explanation.en: Exploring objects with no reward is, in other animals, “usually interpreted as a form of play” → C.
explanation.kk: Сыйсыз заттарды зерттеу басқа жануарларда «usually interpreted as a form of play» → C.
explanation.ru: Исследование предметов без награды у других животных «usually interpreted as a form of play» → C.

items.quote: protections that were formerly reserved for vertebrates
items.prompt: Legal protection for animals used in research

explanation.en: “formerly reserved for vertebrates” — vertebrates are animals with backbones → D.
explanation.kk: «formerly reserved for vertebrates»: vertebrates — омыртқалы жануарлар (backbones) → D.
explanation.ru: «formerly reserved for vertebrates»: vertebrates = животные с позвоночником (backbones) → D.

groups.instruction: Complete each sentence with the correct ending, A–G, from the list below.

items.quote: the problem facing most historic cities was a shortage of visitors rather than a surplus
items.prompt: Until fairly recently, the typical historic city wished it could attract more tourists.

explanation.en: A generation ago the problem was “a shortage of visitors rather than a surplus” → YES.
explanation.kk: Бір ұрпақ бұрын мәселе «a shortage of visitors rather than a surplus» болған → YES.
explanation.ru: Поколение назад проблемой была «a shortage of visitors rather than a surplus» → YES.

items.quote: The debate that has followed is often conducted in slogans, which is a pity, because the evidence is more interesting than either side’s rhetoric
items.prompt: The public argument about tourism generally reflects what the research shows.

explanation.en: The writer says the debate runs on slogans and the evidence is more interesting than the rhetoric. A view is stated, so NO, not NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Автор ашық айтады: талқы ұранмен жүреді, деректер риторикадан қызықтырақ. Пікір бар — бұл NOT GIVEN емес, NO.
explanation.ru: Автор прямо говорит: спор ведётся лозунгами, а данные интереснее риторики сторон. Мнение выражено — это NO, а не NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: How far such charges alter behaviour is disputed
items.prompt: Fees for entering certain districts have cut day trips in most of the cities that charge them.

explanation.en: The writer only says the effect of charges on behaviour “is disputed”; nothing on fewer day trips in most cities → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Автор алымдардың мінез-құлыққа әсері даулы екенін ғана айтады; қалалардың көбінде сапар азайғаны туралы жоқ → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: Автор пишет только, что влияние сборов на поведение спорно; о снижении поездок в большинстве городов ничего нет → NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: the revenue is at least visible to residents
items.prompt: Money raised from visitor charges is something local people can actually see.

explanation.en: “the revenue is at least visible to residents” → YES.
explanation.kk: «the revenue is at least visible to residents» → YES.
explanation.ru: «the revenue is at least visible to residents» → YES.

items.quote: they are also more likely to achieve what residents actually want
items.prompt: Most residents of busy districts would support a fixed cap on the number of tourists.

explanation.en: Flexible tools are closer to what residents want, but whether residents would back a fixed cap is never stated → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Икемді шаралар тұрғындардың қалауына жақын делінген, бірақ олар шекті сан қоюды қолдай ма — айтылмаған → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: Сказано, что гибкие меры ближе к желаниям жителей, но чего именно хотят жители и поддержат ли они потолок — не сказано → NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: treats a cyclist who spends a week in a family guesthouse and a day visitor who spends an afternoon in the busiest square as the same kind of pressure
items.prompt: A single numerical limit treats very different kinds of trip as if they were alike.

explanation.en: A cap on numbers “treats a cyclist … and a day visitor … as the same kind of pressure”, which they are not → YES.
explanation.kk: Сан шегі «treats a cyclist … and a day visitor … as the same kind of pressure, which they plainly are not» → YES.
explanation.ru: Лимит на число «treats a cyclist … and a day visitor … as the same kind of pressure, which they plainly are not» → YES.

groups.instruction: Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Text 3? Write YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writer, NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writer, NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this.

items.quote: he regards limits on short-term letting as more urgent than any restriction on arrivals
items.prompt: Controlling holiday rentals is a higher priority than reducing how many people come.

explanation.en: “limits on short-term letting as more urgent than any restriction on arrivals” is Ferreira → B.
explanation.kk: «limits on short-term letting as more urgent than any restriction on arrivals» — Ferreira → B.
explanation.ru: «limits on short-term letting as more urgent than any restriction on arrivals» — Ferreira → B.

items.quote: since they do not vote in local elections and cannot complain about how they are described
items.prompt: Tourists are an easy target partly because they have no say in local politics.

explanation.en: “they do not vote in local elections” is Raman → C.
explanation.kk: «they do not vote in local elections» — Raman → C.
explanation.ru: «they do not vote in local elections» — Raman → C.

items.quote: will do less good than those that shift visits to other areas and other seasons
items.prompt: Moving visits to other places and seasons would achieve more than cutting the overall figure.

explanation.en: Solberg: cutting the total “will do less good than those that shift visits” → A. Okafor spreads ship calls across the week, a narrower point.
explanation.kk: Solberg: жалпы санды азайту «will do less good than those that shift visits» → A. Okafor кемелерді апта бойына бөлу туралы айтады.
explanation.ru: Solberg: сокращение общего числа «will do less good than those that shift visits» → A. У Okafor речь о распределении судов по неделе, а не о тоталах.

items.quote: an outright ban, which in his view would simply move the ships to a neighbouring port with fewer controls
items.prompt: Prohibiting one form of arrival would simply push the problem somewhere nearby.

explanation.en: “an outright ban … would simply move the ships to a neighbouring port” is Okafor → D.
explanation.kk: «an outright ban … would simply move the ships to a neighbouring port» — Okafor → D.
explanation.ru: «an outright ban … would simply move the ships to a neighbouring port» — Okafor → D.

groups.instruction: Look at the following statements and the list of people below. Match each statement with the correct person, A–D.

items.quote: Annual figures, she points out, can therefore look moderate while particular streets are overwhelmed for part of every day
items.prompt: According to Solberg, why can yearly visitor statistics give a false impression?

options.text: They leave out visitors who stay with friends.
They hide the crowding of certain streets at certain times.
They are collected by the tourism industry.
They count some passengers twice.

explanation.en: “Annual figures … can therefore look moderate while particular streets are overwhelmed” → B.
explanation.kk: «Annual figures … can therefore look moderate while particular streets are overwhelmed» → B.
explanation.ru: «Annual figures … can therefore look moderate while particular streets are overwhelmed» → B.

items.quote: a district that remains full of people but has lost its population
items.prompt: What point is Ferreira making about central areas affected by holiday rentals?

options.text: They are empty for most of the year.
They stay busy but lose the people who lived there.
Their old buildings have been pulled down.
Their shops have all closed.

explanation.en: “remains full of people but has lost its population”: crowded, but the residents have gone → B.
explanation.kk: «remains full of people but has lost its population»: адам көп, бірақ тұрғындар қалмаған → B.
explanation.ru: «remains full of people but has lost its population»: людей много, но жителей не осталось → B.

items.quote: because most of their meals and accommodation are provided on board, the city receives the crowds with relatively little of the spending
items.prompt: Why, in Okafor’s view, do cruise ships create particular difficulties for ports?

options.text: They arrive without warning.
Passengers spend little in the city because the ship supplies their needs.
They damage harbour walls.
Their passengers stay for several days.

explanation.en: Meals and beds are “provided on board”, so the city gets the crowds without much of the spending → B.
explanation.kk: Тамақ пен жатын орын «provided on board», сондықтан қалаға қаражатсыз көп адам келеді → B.
explanation.ru: Еда и жильё «provided on board», поэтому городу достаются толпы почти без расходов туристов → B.

items.quote: The cities that have made most progress are those that stopped counting arrivals and started measuring what the arrivals were doing to the places they came to see
items.prompt: What is the writer’s overall conclusion?

options.text: Tourism should be reduced in every historic city.
What visitors do, and where, matters more than how many arrive.
Cruise traffic is the main cause of overcrowding.
Visitor charges have solved the problem in several cities.

explanation.en: Progress came to cities that “stopped counting arrivals and started measuring what the arrivals were doing” → B.
explanation.kk: Ең жақсы нәтиже «stopped counting arrivals and started measuring what the arrivals were doing» дегендерде → B.
explanation.ru: Лучшие результаты у городов, которые «stopped counting arrivals and started measuring what the arrivals were doing» → B.
